PREFACE
The New Jersey Historical Records Survey Project was organized February
1936 , as a unit of the Works Progress Administration . It operated as a
statewide project under the local sponsorship of the New Jersey State Plan-
ning Board . Until the war forced suspension of its peacetime program , the
technical supervision of the Survey was exercised nationally by Mr. Sargent
B. Child , National Director . State administrative supervision is provided
by Mrs. Eva H. Reda -Reina . The project was under the additional supervision
of Mr. R. C. Branion , Regional Director of PA .
This Survey had as its objective the preparation of complete inventor-
ies of the municipal , county , State and Federal archives in New Jersey , and
the publication of these inventories as guides to the material of greatest
historical interest . In addition to these inventories , the work included
the cataloging and calendaring of manuscript collections , the inventorying
of church archives , and the transcription of ecme of the earliest public and
church records . An additional feature of this comprehensive approach to
authentic historical source material was found in the inventorying of Ameri-
can imprints and portraits in New Jersey ,
The Survey was also engaged in compiling the monumental Atles of Con-
gressional Roll -Calls : An Analysis of Yea -Nay Votes , mapping , with analyses ,
roll calls , and index of all the yea -nay votes in the Congress of the
United States from 1775 - 1932. It was continuing the collection of the
Messages and Papers of the Presidents , i.e. the messages , communications ,
proclamations , executive and administrative orders of the Presidents since
January 21 , 1937 , bringing up to date the original compilation initiated
by the Survey in New York . It maintained a cumulative list and index of
all Presidential Executive Orders of the Unnumbered Series , containing all
the entries in this bock to which additional entries were to be added as
discovered . It prepared a handbook of Federal District and Circuit Courts ,
consisting of maps showingthe evolution of their jurisdiction , tables of
all times and places of meeting , and complete rosters of their judges .
The legislative ordinances of the Continental Congresses and She Congresses
of the Confederation were being compiled for the first time , in a format
based on that used in the United States Statutes at Large . Revised and up
to date rosters cf all members of the Congress of the United States from
1789 to date were also in preparation , and compilations of Presidential
Executive Orders and Proclamations for twelve special topics , including
Passport Regulations , Consular Regulations , Wildlife Conservation , Alien En-try Regulations , and National Forests were being assembled in order that tris
valuable and useful material might be made available to the public in ts
most usable form . All these work phares were handled by the Congressional
Vote Analysis Unit under the technical direction of Clifford L. Lord , Con-
sultant to the Survey , as Editor . To Mr. Lord must be accorded the ack-
nowledgement of the Survey for planning and directing the execution of all
editorial work in these phases , and for preparing the completed work for
final publication . This publication , List and Index of the Praiential
Executive Order . Unnumbered Series , is the second of this series to be
issued by the Survey to date .
Recent important administrative usage of the Presidential Executive

iii
Order has centered new interest and appreciation on this form of govern-
ment document . Today every such order must be filed with the Division of
the Federal Register ( formerly with the Department of State ) in Washing-
ton , and approximately 8,500 orders have been so filed . Then deposited
with this agency , the orders are given official numbers , and thenceforth
may be classified as being in the " numbered series " . Many of these are
now published in the Federal Register daily . But in earlier days , through
administrative laxity , considerably less than half the Presidential orders
were filed with the State Department , and the bulk of the earlier orders
therefore received no official numbers . They constitute the " unnumbered
series" , of , which this volume constitutes the first comprehensive list and
index . A similar list and index of the orders of the numbered series is
in preparation by the Historical Records Survey in New York City . Num-
bered and Unnumbered orders cover exactly the same fields . Both types are
equally important . The only distinction that can be made between them is
this arbitrary one , the state of being numbered , which depends entirely on
whether or not the State Department received a copy for its files .
The total of unnumbered orders is unknown . Secretary of the Interior ,
Harold L. Ickes , once put it at fifteen thousand . Other estimates have run
as high as fifty thousand . This volume , therefore , covers a very small por-
tion of the total field . Thousands of additional orders are scattered
throughout the early departmental files in Washington , and are not readily
accessible . Others exist in collections of Presidential papers elsewhere
in the country . It has seemed , therefore , worthwhile to make this prelimi-
nary list and index of such of the unnumbered orders as are known to exist .
As additional orders come to light , it is to be hoped that they may
be added to such a list and index as this , so that eventually this great
body of material may be opened to the American scholar and public servant .
This Survey would welcome any suggestions or information as to additional
sources or depositories of such orders for incorporation in future edi-tions of this work .
The thanks of the Survey are extended to Columbia University which ,
through the Department of History and its Library staff , particularly
Dr. C. C. Williamson , Miles 0. Price , and Dorothy M. Peake , has contri-
buted so much to the present volume . The staff of the National Archives
has generously aided the editor in answering many of the questions of in-
correct dating , and other problem entries which occur in the available
printed Orders . To Dr. Philip Hamer is due special thanks . To him goes
the credit for eliminating a number of possible errors . To us belongs the

INTRODUCTION
History of the Executive Order
The Presidential Executive Order in the last fifty years has become
an instrument of broad and increasing importance , a fact made particularly
obvious during the last few years . In use from the earliest days of the
Republic , the Executive Order was at first most employed for the withdrawal
from the public domain of lands for Indian , military , naval and lighthouse
reservations , or other similar public purposes , and for the establishment ,
transfer and abolition of land districts and offices , supplementing acts
of Congress . Later it was used for the creation , alteration or disposit-
ion of forest , oil , gas or coal reserves and for the withdrawal of public
lands from sale or entry for purposes of accurate classification . It be-
came an essential instrument in the evolution of the civil service , blanket-
ing into the classified service additional positions as authorized by law ,
promulgating rules for the service , and making plentiful individual except-
ions and exemptions from these rules , both with and without the approval
of the Civil Service Commission. It was employed to effect various reg-
ulations applying to governmental employees outside as well as inside the
growing classified service . It established days of mourning for the death
of famous citizens . It established and altered certain Indian reservations ,
and extended Indian trust allotment periods . It was used to give public
notice of changes of general interest in the regulations governing the
consular and diplomatic services . Occasionally the Order has been used for
the distribution of quasi - governmental funds such as the Virginius in-
demnity fund . Actual allocations of direct government funds were first
made by Executive Order in the distribution of certain blarket appropri-
ations for the possessions newly acquired duringthe war with Spain .
Customs collection districts and offices , regulations for the early
government of the Canal Zone , establishing army schedules of punishments
and schedules of allowances for subsistence and quarters , soon came within
the field of the Order .
During the World War the use of the Executive Order logically in-
creased as executive authority and power increased , and its scope was
greatly broadened . Government agencies such as the Food Administration ,
the Grain Corporation , the Committee on Public Information and the War
Trade Board , authorized by law, were formally established , while others
were reorganized under the Overman Act . Presidential powers were delegat-
ed to subordinate officers . Appropriations were allocated . Coal prices
were fixed . Censorship of the foreign language press was established .
Defensive sea areas were set up . Rules governing the behavior of enemy
aliens were promulgated . The interned ships and enemy powers were assigned
to various departments and agencies for use . Property in the hands of the
Alien Property Custodian was offered for sale . Non - combatant duties for
conscientious objectors to selective service were defined .

vi
Federal rules for wartime radio broadcasting were established and bullion
exports regulated .
During the administration of Franklin D. Roosevelt , also a period of
great executive authority , the order has seen even wider and more vital
usage , both in the administration of the New Deal , and in the evolution
of the program of national defonse .
Different types of Presidential Orders
The President may issue orders in any of three roles : as the civil
executive carrying out specific authorizations of the Congress , as the ad-
ministrative head of the Executive branch of the government , or as Commander-
in -Chief of the Army and Navy . These different types of Presidential Or-
ders today are known as " Executive " , " Administrative " , and "Military " Or-
ders , respectively . However , prior to the present Administration no dis-
tinction was made between the first two , and many " Executive " orders have
been of an administrative nature . In order that this volume together with
the List and Index of the Orders of the Numbered Series , in preparation
by the Survey in New York , may offer a complete guide to the Executive Or-
der , Administrative Orders of the last few years are here listed , for
though they are orders issued by the civilian Executive of the nation , they
have not been included in the Numbered Series of Executive Orders . This
volume also includes the so - called " Presidential Regulations " which have
recently appeared . These are Executive Orders , but were not so headed
through the inadvertence of the person who drafted the Order , and of the
Bureau of the Budget , and the Department of Justice which today must pass
on every Order prior to its submittal to the President . The List and Index
does not include Military Orders , which are issued under a different author-ity and for very different purposes .
The President may also order one of his Cabinet to issue an Order in
his name , or upon his direction . Such Orders are included in this List ,
provided that the issuing official expressly states that the Order is
issued at the direction or command of the President , and that it is not a
Military Order .
The President also very frequently sends letters or memoranda to his
subordinates , directing them to do some particular thing , or clothing them
with some particular power . These technically may be called " Presidential
Letters " and as such are omitted from this compilation , except for a very
few early letters which have the applicability and general interest of
later Orders , and which have been accepted by earlier compilers of Execu-
tive Orders as being Orders in the modern sense .
Availability of the Executive Orders
Some compilations of Orders have been published on such special subjects
as Indian Reservations , the Panama Canal , the PA , Veterans ' Regulations ,
etc. Civil Service Orders appear both in the Annual Report of the Civil
Service Commission , and in the compilation known as Civil Service Acts ,
Rules , Regulations , etc. though in both compilations , many Orders aregiven only by abstracts of the original . Other orders appear in the United

of Fair Competition , the Reports of the Alien Property Custodian , Emer-
gency Regulations Passed Prior to December 1917 ( Dept. of Justice ) , and
Immigration Laws and Regulations .
The recent Code of Federal Regulations of the United States contains
a listing of all Orders cited anywhere in the Code , arranged both by Code
title , i . e . by subject , and by number . But since the Code contains only

restriction as to " general applicability and legal effect " substantially
limits the number of Orders appearing in the Register . A large number of

a number , whether subsequently published in the Register or not .
A full file of the Orders of the numbered series is maintained in the
State Department records , National Archives , while current Orders are
filed in the Division of the Federal Register . There is also a complete
file of these Orders in the Law Library of Columbia University .
As will immediately be seen , all the above sources represent only par-
tial approaches to the total mass and subject matter of the Executive Or-
ders. Of the great bulk ofthe material in these Orders , there is today
no complete file , no full list , no detailed index .

The Numbered and the Unnumbered Order
As has been stated in the preface , no , distinction can be made be-
tween the numbered and unnumbered Order on the basis of subject matter ,
general applicability , public interest , or legal effect . The sole differ-
ence is an arbitrary one based entirely on whether the given Order does
or does not bear a number .
This numbering was begun by the Department of State in 1907 , at which
time all of the relatively few Orders then on file in that Department were
arranged chronologically and given a number , as was every Order subsequently
filed . Those numbers are recorded in the Documentary Catalog from 1907 on
( 60th Congress ff) . Back Orders later added to this file were given " in-
between " numbers.5
But still many Orders did not make their way into the files of the
State Department , and so did not receive numbers . President Hoover made
a fairly successful attempt to end this situation and to regularize the
preparation and handling of these documents by Executive Order 5220 , of
November 8 , 1929 , in which he outlined a procedure by which drafts of
both proclamations and Orders were , to be sent in triplicate to the White
House via the State Department , each draft bearing a suitable title , and
conforming both to the latest decisions of the United States Geographic
Board on the spelling of geographical terms , and to the rules of the
Style Manual of the Government Printing Office on orthography and punctu-
ation. The State Department was to keep one copy of the draft Order and
the signed original . This Order ( 5220 ) was slightly modified by Executive
Orders 5658 of June 24 , 1931 , and 6427 of August 10 , 1933. Orders approving
NRA codes of fair competition were specifically excepted from this pro-
cedure by Executive Order 6497 of December 15 , 1923. Present procedure is
regulated by Executive Order 7298 of February 18 , 1936 .
The volume of unnumbered Orders was substantially reduced by the num-
bering system inaugurated in 1907. The procedural Orders since November
8 , 1929 , have practically eliminated the unnumbered Order .
Some eighty-nine hundred Executive Orders have so far found a place in
the numbered series . This volume contains entries for over fifteen hundred
unnumbered Orders . The importance of the data embodied , and the actions
taken in these Orders has made this volume seem an addition worth making
to the existing tools for the study of American history , law and govern-
ment . To this material , the List is the calendar or chronological key ,
the Index the topical key .

Varieties of the Executive Order
As anyone who is acquainted with the earlier Executive Orders knows ,
no uniformity of form or style was established prior to 1873 , when in the
second administration of President Grant , the present form of the Order be-
came relatively well established .
This variety of form creates the problem , particularly acute in the
earlier years , of just what is and what is not to be classified correctly
as an Executive Order . Where today the President would issue a formal and
detailed Order based on a draft prepared for his signature by a Cabinet
officer , many of his predecessors merely inscribed the word " Approved " at

The Index
The roader may find the following information useful in consulting
the indox . All entries are arranged alphabetically by topic . Each en-
try ends with a series of figures representing the date of the Order , as
" 1889 : 7-23 " : The date alone may be all a reader wants , or with the date
the reader may refer to the List entry for the Order of that date , and
there obtain the citation or citations with which the text of the Order
itsolf may be found in published compilations . This system provides more
useful , spccific and exact reference than a more page citation to the
List would offer .
•
See references are generally used in order to make it as easy as
possible for the reader to locate the information he is seeking . Every
governmental agency is listed under is full official title , with see
references from the common name or inverted forms of that title . Inde-
pondent agencies , commissions , etc. appear under their own formal titleonly . Bursaus and divisions of the regular Departments are listed under
" U.S. Depart.onts " under subhead by name of the Department , with the sub-
sub -head by none of the purcau or division . Orders applying to Cabinet
officers are grouped under " U.S.Secretaries -- State " , etc. All federal
courts are under " U.S.Courts " , the Army under " U.S. Army " , the Navy under
" U.S.Navy " , the Marine Corps under " U.S. Marine Corps " .
Entries under " Public Domain " are arranged by State , with subhead
by type of withdrawal . Those same entries , except for withdrawals for
classification , mineral leases , and similar administrative Orders , are
duplicated under the keyho d of the tyne of withdrawal . Thus an Order
crcating the Cocopah Indian Reservation in Arizona is listed both under
" Public Domain --Arizona-- Indian Reservations -- Cocopah " and under " Indian
Reservations -- Cocopah , Ariz . " This type of duplication exists for " For-
ests , Tational " , " Game , Bird and fish Preserves " , " Parks , National " , and
"Monuments , National " .
All ontrics to material portaining to the Territories and posses-
sions are indexed only under the name of the Territory or possession .
